**Title:** *Still Life with a Dark Bottle and Lemons*

A dark green-black bottle stands left of centre against a dim umber wall; to its right a shallow white bowl holds two lemons, and a pale pear and a single lemon rest on the warm pool of the tabletop. The light comes from the upper left, so the bottle carries a broad reflection and a thin specular while the fruit hold the brightest notes and cast soft shadows to the right.

This session I worked on dry ground: I repainted the pear as a solid body (it had gone transparent where the table showed through), evened the wall and table, relaid the cast shadows, and gave the bottle one clean vertical lay-in with its reflections. The table edge is drawn behind the bottle, and small speculars finish the fruit.

**Title:** *Still Life with a Dark Bottle and a Bowl of Lemons*

The picture is a still life in a warm, dim key: a tall near‑black glass bottle carrying a soft left reflection and a crisp specular, a white bowl of two lemons, a single lemon at the left edge, and a pear at the right, all ranged along a broad table against a murky brown wall with a glow behind the bottle and the shadows falling short and soft to the lower right.

I found it on the easel in a state the journal had already called finished, but looking at it plainly it was still flat — the fruit were pale blobs carrying a regular stipple mesh, the bowl a white ring, the bottle a muddy silhouette, the table blotchy. So I judged it unfinished and painted on. I repainted the fruit as opaque, rounded bodies with a cored shadow and a warm bounce; gave the bowl an exterior shadow side and a deeper interior; rebuilt the bottle as clean glass; and unified the table and wall, re‑laying the cast shadows and deepening the background so the objects carry the light. A useful lesson along the way: thin films of earth over a pale ground lighten rather than darken, so the shadows had to be built up in several full passes.

**Title:** *Still Life with a Dark Bottle and a Bowl of Lemons*

A tall, near-black bottle stands against a dim warm-grey wall on a broad ochre table; to its right a shallow white bowl holds two lemons, with a pear at the right edge and a single lemon lying at the left to close the composition. The light comes from the upper left, so the bottle carries one soft window reflection and the fruit turn from a lit upper-left into a soft olive shadow with a warm bounce along the lower edge. The picture is built almost entirely from lead white, yellow ochre, raw umber and bone black, with a little smalt cooling the wall — a quiet, low-key arrangement.

It took many campaigns. The hard lessons, recorded in the journal: thin films of earth lighten over a pale base, so shadows have to be built in full passes; soft gradients painted into open paint fuse to mush; nested hard passes posterize into rings; and what finally made the fruit round was a soft-edged mask with clipping, so the lit passage dissolves into the shadow instead of ending on a line.
